cards.title: Market selection: the four indicators
cards.summary: Screen a niche on massive pain, purchasing power, easy targeting and growth before building any offer.
cards.use_when: Choosing or re-evaluating which market or niche to serve with an ecommerce offer.
steps: Score the market on four indicators: (1) Massive pain — they must desperately need, not merely want, what you sell. Pain can be anything that frustrates life: being broke, bad relationships, waiting in line, back pain, weight. The degree of pain is proportional to the price you can charge.

Confirm purchasing power: targets must have the money, or access to it, at the price you need to make it worth your time. A resume-writing service for unemployed people had pain, size and constant new entrants but no ability to pay.

Confirm easy targeting: the avatar should gather somewhere findable — associations, mailing lists, social groups, channels. If finding them is like needles in a haystack, the offer will never reach interested eyes. Ads shown to nursing students do not sell to rich doctors.
Confirm growth: growing markets act as a tailwind; shrinking markets as a headwind. Newspapers scored 3 of 4 for one software vendor but shrank ~25% per year and no effort overcame it.
Test the pain articulation: if you can describe the prospect's pain accurately, they will almost always buy. The source's sales-team maxim is 'the pain is the pitch.'
caveats: The four indicators are a screen, not a guarantee of success.
A 'normal' market — growing at market rate with common unmet needs in health, wealth or relationships — is sufficient; you do not need a once-in-a-lifetime market.

cards.title: Order of leverage: market > offer > persuasion
cards.summary: Rate market, offer strength and persuasion as great/normal/bad and read success off the highest-priority lever first.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a business is or isn't growing, and deciding where to invest effort first.
steps: Rank the three levers in this order of importance: Starving Crowd (market) > Offer Strength > Persuasion Skills.

Rate each on a great / normal / bad scale. A great rating on a higher lever overpowers anything below it; a normal rating passes the burden to the next lever; a bad rating stops the equation unless a great higher component nullifies it.
Scenario A (great market): a bad offer and weak persuasion still make money — e.g. selling hot dogs on the corner when bars close at 2am to a mob of hungry people.
Scenario B (normal market + great offer): a Grand Slam Offer makes large profits even with poor persuasion. This is the scenario the book is written for.
Scenario C (normal market + normal offer): you must be exceptionally good at persuasion to succeed massively; possible, but the hardest path and most effort-intensive.
Conclude that strengthening the offer is a shortcut past the persuasion-dependent path; otherwise you own a normal business that only works with exceptional sales skill.
caveats: The ordering is the source's model, not an empirical law.
You can be in a normal market and still make 'crazy money' — the book's own businesses were all normal markets, per the source, not only outlier situations.

cards.title: Health, wealth and relationships: choosing a subgroup
cards.summary: Start from the three evergreen demand buckets, then pick a growing subgroup that has pain, money and findability.
cards.use_when: Generating niche candidates when you don't yet know who to serve.
steps: Recognize three markets that always exist because lacking them is always painful: Health, Wealth and Relationships. Demand is chronic, so your job is channeling existing demand, not creating it.
List what you are good at within those buckets and who would value it most.
Filter candidates by the strongest combination of pain, buying power and targeting, and check the market isn't shrinking.

Worked example from the source: an advisor could serve general relationship coaching or coach second-half-of-life relationships. Seniors who are alone tend to feel more pain (nearer death), have more buying power, and are easy to find; and at the time of writing more people turned 65 each year than 20.
Once three criteria are strong and the market isn't shrinking, proceed — this is enough to be in good shape.
caveats: The source's demographic claim about 65- vs 20-year-olds is time-stamped to the writing and should be re-verified for your market.
Health/wealth/relationships is a starting taxonomy, not a demand-validation test.

cards.title: Commit to the niche — avoid niche slap
cards.summary: Pick one market and stay long enough to iterate; switching niches restarts your learning curve and forfeits compounding.
cards.use_when: When tempted to abandon a niche because it hasn't yet produced the desired revenue.
steps: Treat a failed first offer as a failed offer, not a failed market. Most niches classed as 'bad' are normal markets worth billions where the entrepreneur simply hasn't found a Grand Slam Offer yet.
Do not hop from dentists to chiropractors to escape problems. Both are normal markets and represent large revenue, but you must pick one — no one can serve two masters.
Accept that all markets have unpleasant characteristics; the grass is not greener on the other side.

Stay with your choice long enough to run trial and error. You will fail; you will fail until you succeed, and you will fail far longer if you change who you market to, because each switch starts you over from the beginning.
Re-frame failure: your offer failing does not mean you fail. It means the offer needs work. You only fail if you stop trying.

Set an explicit example of specificity for reference: the source's chosen avatar was a microgym owner with ~100 members, a signed lease, at least one employee, wanting to help clients lose weight. That business turned down non-matching buyers (personal trainers, online coaches) to keep messaging and product focus sharp.
caveats: Refusing mismatched buyers is the source's own practice for Gym Launch, not a universal rule for every business.
The commit advice is framed for entrepreneurs below $10M/year; the source notes broadening may become relevant above that depending on total addressable market.

cards.title: Niche pricing: the same product can sell for 100x
cards.summary: Successive levels of niche specificity let you charge multiples more for a nearly identical core product.
cards.use_when: Deciding how narrowly to define an offer's audience and how that changes justifiable price.
steps: Recognize that specificity raises willingness to pay because a single relevant sale or outcome becomes easy to justify against price.

Walk the ladder from the source: a generic 'Time Management' course ~$19; 'Time Management for Sales Professionals' ~$99; 'Time Management for B2B Outbound Sales Reps' ~$499, where one extra sale can net the buyer $500+; 'Time Management for B2B Outbound Power Tools & Gardening Sales Reps' ~$1,000–$2,000.

Apply the same ladder to services: a generic weight-loss fitness program might be $19–$199 while a program designed and marketed only to shift nurses might be $1,997, even though both reduce to eat less and move more.

Aim to be 'the guy' who services this type of person or solves this type of problem, and ideally: I solve this problem for this specific person in this counter-intuitive way that reverses their deepest fear.
caveats: The price figures are illustrations of the mechanism, not benchmarks to copy.
Either market is workable; the source insists you cannot serve both at once.
The source advises niching down for most businesses under $10M/year; above that, broadening depends on total addressable market.

cards.title: Do not compete on price
cards.summary: The default pricing process copies dead-broke competitors and leads to a race to the bottom; close the value-price gap instead.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to lower prices to stay competitive or to raise the value delivered.
steps: Spot the common pattern: look at the marketplace, see what everyone offers, take the average, go slightly below to stay competitive, add 'a little more', and end up with 'more for less'. The competitors being copied are, in the source's words, dead broke.

Understand that pricing where the market is means pricing for market efficiency: more competitors enter with more-for-less until no one can offer any more for any less, and operators make just enough to keep the month going.
Note the consequence: the bottom 10–20% of operators get washed out, new owners enter and repeat the cycle.

Instead, first raise the value delivered, then raise price — 'we will raise our price only after we have sufficiently increased our value' — so buyers still receive a deal, e.g. $100,000 of value for $10,000.
Adopt the source's aim: not the most customers, but the most money, and the only way down is to $0 while value can rise indefinitely.
caveats: This is a strong opinion attributed to the source; a strategy of being second-cheapest has no strategic benefit, per Dan Kennedy as quoted, but situations vary.
Lowering price is only appropriate if you have a revolutionary way to cut costs to roughly one-tenth of competitors — otherwise don't.

cards.title: The virtuous cycle of price
cards.summary: Lower prices corrode client investment, results and margin; higher prices increase investment, perceived value, results and margin.
cards.use_when: Justifying a price increase to yourself or clients, or diagnosing poor client results.
steps: Map what happens when you decrease price: less emotional investment from clients, lower perceived value (it cannot be that good if so cheap), worse results because they are uninvested, attraction of the most dissatisfied clients, and destroyed margin for hiring, experience, tooling and scale — your world and often the service itself gets worse.

Map the reverse when you raise price: more emotional investment, higher perceived value, better results because they are invested, better and easier-to-satisfy clients who often cost less to fulfill, and multiplied margin to invest in systems, people and scale.

Apply to any service where the customer must act to get the result: the more invested they are, the more likely they achieve the positive outcome. Price to create a sting that focuses attention — 'those who pay the most, pay the most attention.'
Use the wine study as an illustration: participants rated the same wine higher when they believed it was expensive, so raising price can increase experienced value without changing the product.
caveats: The wine result is a single cited study used as illustration, not a promise for your product.
Charging premium demands delivery: the source says you must outwork self-doubt and have conviction from repeatedly producing results, or you will fail.
The 'attract the worst clients' claim is the source's framing; treat it as situational, not absolute.

cards.title: Aim to be a category of one
cards.summary: Price so far above the market that buyers assume something categorically different is happening, creating monopoly-like positioning.
cards.use_when: Setting a premium price point and positioning the offer against existing competitors.
steps: Benchmark the market: identify the low-price players and the highest-price player.

In the source's example, when entering the gym market, low-price competitors charged $500/month for full-service marketing and the one high-price competitor charged $5,000. They priced at three times the highest player and 32 times the low-price players: $16,000 for a 16-week done-with-you intensive.
Then build an upsell: 35% of those buyers moved into a three-year, $42,000/year agreement — a large commitment relative to the average gym owner's take-home profit of $35,280/year.

Price so high that a consumer thinks 'this is so much more expensive, there must be something entirely different going on here' — that creates a category of one, a perceived monopoly, and monopoly profits.

Support it with proof: a voluntary survey of 158 gyms reported average 11-month improvements of +$19,932/month topline, +$13,339/month recurring revenue, profit from $2,943/month to $8,940/month, +67 clients, churn from 10.7% to 6.8%, and retail sales +$4,400/month.
caveats: These figures are one company's voluntary survey results — examples, not promises.
The 3x-highest / 32x-lowest multipliers and the price points are case specifics, not recommended targets.
Commitment relative to client income was high; the source attributes conversion to conviction built on repeated delivery.

cards.title: Value equation: raise the top, zero the bottom
cards.summary: Value = (dream outcome × perceived likelihood of achievement) ÷ (time delay × effort and sacrifice).
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing an offer to see which of four drivers to improve.
steps: Increase the two top drivers: Dream Outcome and Perceived Likelihood of Achievement.
Decrease the two bottom drivers: Perceived Time Delay Between Start and Achievement, and Perceived Effort & Sacrifice.

Answer the four buyer questions in the prospect's mind: What will I make? (dream outcome) How will I know it will happen? (likelihood) How long will it take? (time delay) What is expected of me? (effort and sacrifice).

Note the formula is a division deliberately: if the bottom can approach zero, value approaches infinity, regardless of how modest the top is. The hypothetical limit is a product where purchase and result are simultaneous — click buy, instantly get the outcome.

Shift effort toward the bottom half. The source says big claims on the top are easy and lazy, while immediacy, seamlessness and lack of effort are what the best companies (Apple, Amazon, Netflix) compete on.
caveats: The 'divide by zero is infinite value' framing is a heuristic, not literal math — the source notes it is technically undefined.
For two offers satisfying the same desire, the dream outcome cancels out and price differences come from the other three variables.

cards.title: Perception is reality: engineer perceived value
cards.summary: Improvements only create value when the prospect perceives them — communication is part of the product.
cards.use_when: When your product objectively solves the problem but prospects don't buy or don't value it.
steps: Accept that increasing likelihood of success or cutting time and effort does nothing for value until the prospect perceives the increase or decrease.

Use the London Underground example: the biggest gain in rider satisfaction came not from faster trains but from a dotted map showing when the next train arrives — a few-million-dollar perceptual fix beating billion-dollar engineering.
Increase perceived likelihood of achievement through messaging, proof, third-party edification, what you include or exclude, and guarantees.
Prefer psychological solutions over logical ones. Logical fixes have usually been tried, because that is what everyone would try, so only the psychological problems remain.

Apply the pattern: instead of faster trains, a dotted map; instead of faster elevators, floor-to-ceiling mirrors so riders are distracted; instead of a discount, make fewer and raise the price so people want it more.
caveats: Sources for these examples include Rory Sutherland of Ogilvy as cited by the author; treat them as illustrations.
Perceptual work still requires real delivery — the source insists the product must perform.

cards.title: Dream outcome: sell status, not features
cards.summary: The dream outcome is the gap between current reality and an envisioned future, and status gain is its strongest driver.
cards.use_when: Writing the promise of an offer and choosing which benefits to lead with.
steps: Identify the stable desires behind purchases: to be perceived as beautiful, respected, powerful, loved, and to increase status. Your job is to channel these desires, not create them.

Frame benefits as status gained in the eyes of others. Instead of 'your drive increases 40 yards,' write: your golf buddies' jaws will drop when your ball soars past theirs; they'll ask what changed, and only you will know.

Understand that many vehicles satisfy the same desire — makeup, anti-aging creams, supplements, shapewear, surgery and fitness all channel 'be perceived as beautiful' — and that the underlying driver is often status within one's social group.
Choose categories by status impact: many men value offers that make money over offers that make them handsome, because money drives status more.

Answer the comparison question: if two offers make someone beautiful, what makes one worth $50,000 and another $5? The difference lies in likelihood, time delay and effort — the other three variables.
caveats: The status framing is the source's generalizing claim; the Lamborghini/minivan anecdote comes via Russell Brunson's account and is illustrative.
Avoid inventing status claims your product cannot credibly support.

cards.title: Perceived likelihood: sell certainty and experience
cards.summary: Buyers pay for confidence that the result will happen; proof, track record and guarantees raise that confidence.
cards.use_when: Deciding what social proof, guarantees or inclusions to place in an offer.
steps: Accept that people pay for certainty: ask how much more someone would pay for a plastic surgeon's 10,000th patient versus their first. The surgery and time are the same; only perceived likelihood of getting the desired result changes — and people might even demand payment to be the first patient.
Raise perceived likelihood through four levers: messaging, proof, what you include or exclude in the offer, and guarantees.
Use third-party edification and track records rather than bigger promises, which are the easiest claims to make and therefore least differentiating.
Note that experience on the provider's side does not itself create value — the buyer must perceive the likelihood of their own achievement.
caveats: The surgeon comparison is an analogy; healthcare pricing and claims are heavily regulated, so claims must be substantiated.
Guarantees are discussed in the source as a value lever; their specific design is covered elsewhere.

cards.title: Time delay: engineer fast wins early
cards.summary: Cut the perceived wait and deliver an emotional win as close to purchase as possible to carry clients to the long-term outcome.
cards.use_when: Designing onboarding, first-week experience or the front end of a service.
steps: Separate the long-term outcome (the dream outcome clients buy) from the short-term experience (the milestones that keep them long enough to reach it).
Tie in as many short-term milestones as possible; people buy the dream but stay for the benefits they discover along the way.

Deliver a big emotional win as close to purchase as possible. Source example: adding $239,000/year to a gym takes time, so they get ads live and the client's first $2,000 sale closed within seven days to reinforce the decision and build trust.
For a 12-month body transformation, recognize the interim benefits — higher energy, higher sex drive, a community — as retention mechanics, not the pitch.
The faster and more clearly you demonstrate those interim benefits, the more valuable the service becomes.
caveats: Fast wins must be genuine; the source frames the early win as proof the path works, not as theater.
Not every offer can compress time to value — the goal is to reduce the perceived delay, not fake immediacy.

cards.title: Effort and sacrifice: remove what the client must do
cards.summary: Lower the work and trade-offs required of the buyer, and treat perceived effort as equally important as actual effort.
cards.use_when: When clients fail to get results because the process is too demanding, or when comparing offers with identical outcomes.
steps: Treat effort and sacrifice as a divisor on value: the same outcome delivered with less client work is worth more.
Benchmark against firms that made things immediate and seamless — the source cites Apple's phone, Amazon's one-click purchase and Netflix's on-demand viewing.

Take the source's own pivot as proof of the mechanism: originally the consulting team flew to gyms and did everything for them (done-for-you) at peak eight turnarounds a month, collecting 100% of incremental revenue — a logistical nightmare. When one gym had to do the work itself with remote guidance, it made nearly $44,000 in new up-front cash sales within 30 days (4x its prior month). Removing the travel constraint let the business sell 4,000+ more gyms on a done-with-you model.
When designing your offer, ask what the client must do — including waiting, learning, coordinating and risk-bearing — and remove or outsource as much as possible.
caveats: The done-with-you transition is a case example; the source's results came with a system the client executed.
Effort reduction can be outweighed by other value drivers; always evaluate the whole equation.

cards.title: Price far above fulfillment cost
cards.summary: Charge much more than it costs you to fulfill — the source suggests up to 100x — as long as the buyer still gets a deal.
cards.use_when: Setting margin targets and defending a large spread between cost and price.
steps: Abandon notions of 'what's fair' in pricing. The source's examples: phone companies add users at pennies and charge hundreds monthly; pharmaceuticals cost pennies to manufacture and sell for hundreds; media companies sell your attention for a king's ransom.
Aim for a large discrepancy between fulfillment cost and price — think up to a hundred times, not two or three times.
At the same time, keep the buyer's value-to-price gap large, so the offer remains a steal: you can sell $100,000 of value for $10,000, described as money at a discount.

Anchor the buyer's economics to their outcome, not your cost: the source's pitch to a gym owner was paying $42,000 against an average $239,000 topline increase over 11 months, roughly 15 hours a week, paid as the money came in — which made the decision obvious even to a skeptical observer.

Track what buyers actually vote for: a photography client raised average ticket from $300 to $1,500 over two years, which multiplied weekly profit from $1,000 to $38,000 while spending less time per customer and reporting higher satisfaction.
caveats: These are the source's case results — examples, not expected outcomes.
Never charge more than the product is worth; the source says both a high cost-to-price spread and a large buyer value-to-price gap are required.
The $1,200,000/month profit figure the author cites is autobiographical and not a benchmark.

cards.title: Repackage the same core into a premium offer
cards.summary: Identify the element buyers value most, triple down on it, and cut everything else to raise price and satisfaction together.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing product to justify a price increase without inventing new features.
steps: Study what customers actually value and vote for with dollars, rather than assuming value.

Triple down on the highest-value element and ruthlessly eliminate everything else; the source attributes a photography client's shift from $300 to $1,500 average ticket to exactly this, noting less time per customer and higher satisfaction alongside it.
Accept that the underlying mechanics may not change (weight loss programs still reduce to eating less and moving more) — repackaging is about specificity, messaging and the value drivers.
Repeat the mechanism across categories: the same principles delivered to a more specific type of person justify more price when tied to one more sale, one more deal, or one avoided problem.
caveats: Raising price without changing perceived value risks breaking the buyer's value-to-price deal.
Satisfaction and time savings are the source's reported outcomes for one client, not guaranteed by repackaging.

cards.title: Raise prices before you think you've earned it
cards.summary: The source claims 99% of businesses should raise prices rather than lower them, because profit funds delivery quality and growth.
cards.use_when: When growth has stalled and discounting seems like the only lever left.
steps: Check the premise: lower price closes the value-price gap but destroys the margin needed to deliver a great experience, hire and retain good people, invest in systems and scale.
Use profit as oxygen for the fire of growth — the source states profit funds reinvestment and ultimately more people helped, not fewer.
Build conviction before raising price: the source says you must deliver repeatedly until you know a given customer will succeed, then let that experience make the ask natural.
Treat price increases as a moral position in the source's framing: premium margin is what lets you serve clients better than competitors who squeeze blood from a stone.
Ignore marketplace pressure that pushes you back toward average; the source says competitors will keep inducing you to lower price and you must resist.
caveats: '99% of businesses should raise prices' is the source's strong opinion, not a universal rule; a product that fails to deliver cannot be rescued by price alone.
Charging premium requires conviction earned through repeated delivery; the source warns against shortcutting the real work.

cards.title: Diagnosing the real constraint: when the market, not the offer, is the problem
cards.summary: A great product, offer and sales skill still fail in a shrinking market; the same operator won by changing markets.
cards.use_when: When you have tested product, offer, marketing and sales and growth still stalls.
steps: Run an explicit diagnosis: is it product, offer, marketing and sales, or team? In the source's newspaper case, the product was strong, the offer was zero-risk revenue share (if the paper made nothing, neither did the vendor), and the founder was a natural salesman.

Check the market's trajectory: newspapers were shrinking ~25% per year. All four market indicators except growth were present — pain, purchasing power and easy targeting — and the shrinking market overrode them.
Recognize the bias that keeps you stuck: entrepreneurs dislike quitting and are accustomed to solving impossible problems, so they keep hitting the same wall.

Consider the pivot proof point: the same founder started automated mask manufacturing during COVID, brought cost per mask below the Chinese purchase price, and reached millions per month within five months — same skillset, zero experience, different market.
Conclude that if the market is shrinking, changing the offer will not fix it; assess the market first, then commit, then iterate the offer.
caveats: The mask-manufacturing outcome is a specific historical case, not a repeatable strategy.
Do not use 'the market is bad' as an excuse to abandon a normal market too early — the source warns against niche-hopping.

But because the crowd was so big and so starving, rolls of toilet paper were going for $100 or more. That’s the value of a starving crowd. Selling Newspapers A good friend of mine, Lloyd, owned a software business that served newspapers for almost a decade. They set up digital ad services on newspaper websites with a few clicks and instantly helped them sell a whole new ad product. He only charged them a percentage of the revenue he added. So if they made nothing, neither did he. It was pure gain for the papers and a great offer. But, despite having a great offer and natural sales ability, his business began to decline. Being a high-achieving entrepreneur, he tried all the different angles to solve the problem — but nothing worked. He couldn't figure out what the issue was. It was hard for me to see him struggle with this because I think Lloyd is much smarter than I am, and the answer seemed obvious to me. But watching him go through this has been a lesson I have taken with me for life.

 Before I reveal it, what do you think the problem was? Product? Offer? Marketing and sales? His team? Let’s break it down. It wasn’t his product — that was great. It wasn’t his offer — he had a zero risk revshare model. It wasn’t his sales skills — he was a natural salesman. So, then what was the problem? He was selling to newspapers! His market was shrinking by 25 percent every year! He had looked at all the angles, except for the most obvious one. Finally, after years of fighting an uphill battle in his market, he realized his market was the source of his problems and decided to downsize his company. Don’t worry — this story has a second half. To illustrate the power of a market, as soon as COVID hit, Lloyd pivoted. He started an automated mask manufacturing company. With new technology, he brought the cost per mask below what people could buy them for from China. Within five months he was doing millions per month. Same entrepreneur. Different market. He applied his same skill set to a business he had zero experience in and was able to win. That’s the power of picking the right market. I give you that story as a cautionary tale. Your market matters. Lloyd is a very smart human. He is obviously very capable. But we can all be blinded as entrepreneurs because we don't like to give up. We are so accustomed to solving impossible problems that we will keep ramming our heads into the wall. We hate quitting. But the reality is that everyone is affected by their market. So how do you pick the right market? What To Look For There is a market in desperate need of your abilities. You need to find it. And when you do, you will capitalize, all while wondering what took you so long. Don’t be romantic about your audience. Serve the people who can pay you what you’re worth. And remember that picking a market, like anything, is always our choice, so choose wisely. In order to sell anything, you need demand. We are not trying to create demand. We are trying to channel it. That is a very important distinction. If you don’t have a market for your offer, nothing that follows will work. This entire book sits atop the assumption that you have at least a “normal” market, which I define as a market that is growing at the same rate as the marketplace and that has common unmet needs that fall into one of three categories: improved health, increased wealth, or improved relationships. For example Lloyd, from the above newspaper story, could have gone through this entire book and nothing in here would have worked for him. Why? Because he would be targeting newspapers, a dying market. That being said, having a great market is an advantage. But you can be in a normal market that’s growing at an average rate and still make crazy money. Every market I have been in has been a normal market. You just don't actually want to be selling ice to eskimos. Here are the basic tenets of what I look for in markets. Let’s run through them before we return to the offer. When picking markets, I look for four indicators: 1) Massive Pain They must not want, but desperately need, what I am offering. Pain can be anything that frustrates people about their lives. Being broke is painful. A bad marriage is painful. Waiting in line at the grocery stores is painful. Back pain . . . ugly smile pain . . . overweight pain . . . Humans suffer a lot. So for us entrepreneurs, endless opportunity abounds. The degree of the pain will be proportional to the price you will be able to charge (more on this in the Value Equation chapter). When they hear the solution to their pain, and inversely, what their life would look like without this pain, they should be drawn to your solution. I have a saying I use to train sales teams “The pain is the pitch.” If you can articulate the pain a prospect is feeling accurately, they will almost always buy what you are offering. A prospect must have a painful problem for us to solve and charge money for our solution. Pro Tip The point of good writing is for the reader to understand. The point of good persuasion is for the prospect to feel understood. 2) Purchasing Power A friend of mine had a very good system for helping people improve their resumes to get more job interviews. He was great at it. But try as he did, he just could not get people to pay for his services. Why? Because they were all unemployed! This, again, may seem obvious. But he thought, “These people are easy to target. They’re in massive pain. There are plenty of them, and it's constantly adding new people. This is a great market!” He just forgot a crucial point: your audience needs to be able to afford the service you’re charging them for. Make sure your targets have the money, or access to the amount of money, needed to buy your services at the prices you require to make it worth your time. 3) Easy to Target Let’s say you have a perfect market, but no way of finding the people who comprise it. Well, making a Grand Slam Offer will be difficult. I make my life easier by looking for easy-to-target markets. Examples of this are avatars that have associations they belong to, mailing lists, social media groups, channels they all watch, etc. If our potential customers are all gathered together somewhere, then we can market to them. If searching them out, however, is like finding needles in a haystack, then it can be very difficult to get your offer in front of any potentially interested eyes. This point is tactical. It is reality, not theoretical. For instance, you may want to serve rich doctors. But if your ads are being displayed to nursing students, your offer will fall on deaf ears, no matter how good it is. Main point: you want to make sure you can target your ideal audience easily. (Clarifying point - there is no issue wanting to serve rich doctors, they are easy to find. This is just illustrative that your promotions must be served to the right audience). 4) Growing Growing markets are like a tailwind. They make everything move forward faster. Declining markers are like headwinds. They make all efforts harder. This was Lloyd's example. Newspapers had three of the four makings of a great market: (1) lots of pain, (2) purchasing power, (3) easy to target. But they were shrinking (fast). No matter how hard he tried, the entire marketplace was fighting against him. Business is hard enough, and markets move quickly. So you might as well find a good market to give you a tailwind to make the process easier. Making This Real There are three main markets that will always exist: Health, Wealth, and Relationships. The reason that those will always exist is that there is always tremendous pain when you lack them. There is always demand for solutions to these core human pains. The goal is to find a smaller subgroup within one of those larger buckets that is growing, has the buying power, and is easy to target (the other three variables). So if I were a relationship expert trying to find my avatar, I’d rather focus on “second half of life relationship” coaching for old timers than helping college students in relationships. Why? Because senior citizens who are alone are likely suffering more pain as they are nearer their deaths (pain), have more buying power (money), and are easy to find (targeting). Lastly, at the time of this writing, there are more people turning 65 each year than turning 20 (growing). That is the idea. Think about what you are good at in regards to health, wealth, and relationships. Then think about who might value your service the most (is in the most pain), has the buying power to pay what you want (money), and can be found easily (targeting). As long as those three criteria are strong and the market isn't shrinking, you’ll be in good shape. But how important to your success is finding a “great market” versus a “normal market” versus a “bad market?” The answer: it actually depends. Let me explain. Order of Importance: Three Levers on Success It’s unlikely you are going to be in a dying market like the newspaper example. It’s also unlikely you’re going to be selling toilet paper in COVID (buying frenzy). You’ll likely be in a “normal” market. And that’s totally okay. There is a fortune to be made within normal markets. My single point here is that you can't be in a “bad” market, or nothing will work. That being said, here’s the simplest illustration of the order of importance between markets, offers, and persuasion skills: Starving Crowd (market) > Offer Strength > Persuasion Skills Let’s say you were to rate these elements on a scale of great, normal, and bad. You could essentially move down the line from left to right in order of importance. A “great” rating on a higher-order piece overpowers anything else lower on the priority scale. A “normal” rating moves the buck to the next part of the equation. A “bad” stops the equation unless a “great” from a higher priority component nullifies it. Here are a few examples: Example #1: Even if you have a bad offer and are bad at persuasion, you’re going to make money if you’re in a great market. If you’re on the corner hocking hot dogs when the bars close up at 2am, with mobs of starving drunk folks, you’re gonna sell out your hotdogs. Example #2 (most of us): If you are in a normal market and have a Grand Slam Offer (great), you can make tons of money even if you’re bad at persuasion. This is most people reading this book. That’s why I wrote it — to help you maximize your success by learning to really build a Grand Slam Offer. Example #3: Let’s say you’re in a normal market and have a normal offer. In order to be massively successful, you would have to be exceptionally good at persuasion. Then and only then will you succeed, with your persuasive skills serving as the fulcrum of your success. Heck, many empires have been built by exceptional persuaders. It’s just the hardest path to follow and requires the most effort and learning. Nailing your offer helps you shortcut this path to success. Otherwise, you will just have a normal business that takes exceptional skill to be successful (nothing wrong with that, but probably not what you signed up for). Commit to the Niche I have a saying when coaching entrepreneurs on picking their target market “Don’t make me niche slap you.” Too often, a newer entrepreneur half-heartedly tries one offer in one market, doesn't make a million dollars, then mistakenly thinks “this is a bad market.” Most times that’s not actually the case. They just haven’t found a Grand Slam Offer yet to apply to that market. They think, I’ll switch from helping dentists to helping chiropractors — that’s it! When, in reality, both of those are normal markets and represent billions of dollars in revenue. Either would work, just not both. You must pick one. No one can serve two masters. I have coined the term “niche slap” to remind entrepreneurs in my communities to commit once they pick. All businesses and, all markets, have unpleasant characteristics. The grass is never greener once you get to the other side. If you keep hopping from niche to niche, hoping that the market will solve your problems, you deserve to be niche slapped. You must stick with whatever you pick long enough to have trial and error. You will fail. In fact, you will fail until you succeed. But you will fail far longer if you keep changing who you market to, because you must start over from the beginning each time. So, pick then commit. Riches Are In The Niches The other reason to commit to the niche is because of how much more you will make. Simply put, niching down will make you far more money. Author Note - When To Broaden (Advice For Most People) For most, if you are under $10M per year, niching down will make you more money. After that, it will depend on how narrow the niche is, or, what is called TAM (total addressable market). A business can really only grow to meet the total addressable market. That being said, for most people, getting to $10M per year is already a top .4% achievement (only 1 in 250 businesses achieve this). So for 99.6 percent of readers below $10M per year, it’s almost always easier to serve fewer clients more narrowly. But if you want to go beyond that, you may (depending on the size of your TAM) have to broaden your audience by going up market, down market, or into an adjacent market where your existing services can provide value. For context, many companies expanded to $30M+ per year serving a single niche: Chiropractors, Gyms, Plumbers, Solar, Roofers, Salon Owners, etc. If you are at $1M or $3M, thinking you have capped and must expand, you are wrong. You just need to be better. When I truly grasped how much more profit I was leaving on the table, it changed my life. It was what took me from doing acquisition for anyone to teaching it to a specific avatar. In my instance, I decided on a microgym owner with ~100 members, a signed lease, at least one employee, and wanted to help clients lose weight. It’s the gap between their current reality and their dreams. Our goal is to accurately depict that dream back to them, so they feel understood, and explain how our vehicle will get them there. The dream outcome is simple; it’s the “getting there” where the value gets enhanced or detracted. People generally, and our clients specifically, want: . . . To be perceived as beautiful . . . To be respected . . . To be perceived as powerful . . . To be loved . . . To increase their status These are all powerful drivers. But multiple vehicles may accomplish the same thing. Take the desire “to be perceived as beautiful” for example, here are a lot of things that touch on this desire: Make Up Anti-aging creams/serums Supplements Shapewear Plastic Surgery Fitness → All these vehicles channel the desire to be perceived as beautiful. And if we further unpack the idea of a desire to be beautiful, we see that it may be a surface-level declaration of a deeper desire to achieve higher status in one’s social group. The dream outcome value driver is most prominently used when comparing the relative value between two different desires being satisfied. In general, the dream outcome that most directly increases a prospect’s status will be the one they value most. As such, a prospect may value that entire category of vehicles that satisfy one desire more than another category that satisfies a different desire. For many men, making money is more important than being handsome. Why? Because money drives status for men more than being handsome does. So, in general, they will value all offers that make them money more than offers that help them look good. I once heard Russell Brunson tell a story about this concept. He explained how his wife, Collette, at first hearing about this status concept, rejected it. She claimed she wasn’t driven by status and would never want to drive a Lamborghini. Instead, she favored her minivan. But, after talking further, she revealed it was because driving a Lamborghini would decrease her status amongst her mom friends, while driving a minivan would show she was a good mother (increase in status). So it’s not about the money, it's about the status (the perceived increase or decrease in relative standing when compared to others socially or professionally). Talk in terms of things your prospect believes will increase their status, and you will have your prospects drooling. Pro Tip: Frame benefits in terms of status gained from the viewpoint of others When writing copy, you can make it that much more powerful by talking about how other people will perceive the prospect’s achievement. Connect the dots for them. Example: If you buy this golf club, your drive will increase by 40 yards. Your golf buddies' jaws will drop when they see your ball soar 40 yards past theirs . . . they’ll ask you what’s changed . . . only you will know. That being said, when comparing two products or services that satisfy the same desire, the value from the dream outcomes will cancel out (since they are the same). It will be the other three variables that drive the difference in perceived value, and ultimately price. For example, if we have two products or services that both help make someone beautiful, it will be the likelihood of achievement, time delay, and effort required that will differentiate the perceived value of each offer. Simply put: if two things make someone beautiful, what makes one worth $50,000 and another $5? Answer: The extent of the other three value variables. #2 Perceived Likelihood of Achievement (Goal = Increase) This was the last of the variables I added when trying to think through this framework a few years ago. I just felt like something was missing with only the other three. Then I realized people pay for certainty. They value certainty. I call this “the perceived likelihood of achievement.” In other words, “How likely do I believe it is that I will achieve the result I am looking for if I make this purchase?” For example, how much would you pay to be a plastic surgeon’s 10,000th patient versus their first? If you're a normal, sane person, a lot more. I mean heck, you might even ask them to pay you if you are their first patient ever. So you can see even from this simple example that while the service you are receiving is technically the same, the only thing that changes is your perceived likelihood of getting what you want. Both surgeons take the same amount of time to do the surgery (if anything, the guy who has done it 10,000 times would likely get it done faster and still charge more). The more-experienced surgeon has a track record of achieving a result, which incentivizes their desirability. People value this perceived likelihood of achievement. Increasing a prospect’s conviction that your offer will “actually” work for them, will make your offer that much more valuable even though the work remains the same on your end. So to increase value with all offers, we must communicate perceived likelihood of achievement through our messaging, proof, what we choose to include or exclude in our offer, and our guarantees (more on these later). #3 Time Delay (Goal = Decrease) Time delay is the time between a client buying and receiving the promised benefit. The shorter the distance between when they purchase and they receive value/the outcome, the more valuable your services or product is. There are two elements to this driver of value: Long-term outcome and short-term experience. Many times, there are short-term experiences that occur while en route to the long-term outcomes. They happen “along the way” and provide value. It’s good to understand both. The thing people buy is the long-term value, aka their “dream outcome.” But the thing that makes them stay long enough to get it is the short-term experience. These are little milestones a prospect sees along the way that shows them they are on the right path. We try and tie as many of these as possible into any service we offer. We want clients to have a big emotional win early (as close as possible to their purchase). This gives them the emotional buy in and the momentum to “see it through” to their ultimate goal. For example, it takes a while to add an extra $239,000 per year to a gym. But that’s what they’re buying. So, once they have purchased, we need to create emotional wins fast. One way we do this is to get their ads live and get them to close their first $2,000 sale within their first seven days. By doing this, their decision to work with us is reinforced, and they immediately trust us more. This makes them more likely to follow the rest of our systems and get to their ultimate destination. Pro Tip: Fast Wins Always try and incorporate short-term, immediate wins for a client. Be creative. They just need to know they are on the right path and that they made the right decision trusting you and your business. Let me give you another example. If I sell someone a bikini body, their time delay to realize that outcome may be 12 months or even longer. Along the way, though, as they change their bodies, they may experience higher sex drive, more energy, and an increased community of friends. They aren’t initially buying those things, but those things may become short-term benefits that keep them in the game long enough to achieve their ultimate outcome. They buy the dream, but they stay for the benefits they discover along the way. The faster and more clearly you can demonstrate those benefits, the more valuable your service will be.
